works.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness and Boundary Conditions of Retrieval Practice, Distributed Practice, and Interleaved Practice in Authentic School Classrooms
works.abstract: While retrieval practice, distributed practice, and interleaved practice are considered three promising strategies for how, when, and in what sequence to practice after initial instruction or self-study, little is known about the average effects of these strategies in authentic classrooms in primary and secondary education and their moderators. Therefore, in the present study, we investigated the effectiveness and boundary conditions of retrieval, distributed, and interleaved practice in such classrooms. We did this using a three-level meta-analysis comprising 233 effect sizes from 53 studies (published 2006–2024) including 7,303 participants. We found (a) an average testing effect of g = 0.37, moderated by type of knowledge, posttest format, format matching between practice and test phase, and type of learning outcome, (b) an average spacing effect of g = 0.20, moderated by type of comparison condition, retention interval, the ISI/RI ratio (i.e., the interstudy interval expressed as proportion of the retention interval), and posttest format, and (c) an average interleaving effect of g = 0.40, moderated by provision and timing of feedback. Average effects suggest that the effectiveness of the three strategies extends to authentic school classrooms. Observed moderator patterns suggest that the testing, spacing, and interleaving effects only occur reliably if their underlying cognitive processes are elicited during practice. This, in turn, implies that we need to shift from a one-size-fits-all instructional approach to a context-dependent instructional approach.

works.title: Designing a Gamified Tool: An ADDIE Approach to Capital Market Flashcard Development
works.abstract: Traditional, lecture-based finance courses frequently overwhelm undergraduate students with dense theoretical content, leading to poor knowledge retention, lower overall engagement, and a heavy reliance on last-minute cramming before major assessments. To address these persistent educational challenges, this study details the design, development, and implementation of a mobile-friendly digital flashcard game specifically tailored for an undergraduate Financial Markets and Institutions (FIN) course using the systematic ADDIE instructional design framework. By integrating active recall strategies, custom visual aids, and an algorithm-driven Spaced Repetition System (SRS), the platform transforms passive studying into a dynamic learning process that prompts students to systematically review challenging concepts based on their individual mastery levels. Subject-matter experts rigorously vetted the curriculum content for accuracy and practical relevance prior to deployment, while formative evaluations directly measured student usability, overall engagement, and conceptual comprehension during active coursework. Formative findings, including high expert ratings for content validity and evidence of adaptive scheduling from system logs, suggest that the tool has strong potential to support active recall. However, its effectiveness in improving long-term knowledge retention and reducing academic anxiety will be examined in a subsequent summative evaluation. Ultimately, by documenting the comprehensive analysis, design, and development phases, this study provides instructional designers and finance educators with a practical, replicable blueprint for implementing gamified, technology-enhanced active learning tools across complex capital markets curricula.

works.title: Building learner agency through cognitive science: A year 9 psychology of learning case study
works.abstract: This case study examines the impact of a Psychology of Learning module within a Year 9 Psychological Literacy course, designed to build learner agency through the explicit teaching of cognitive science. The module introduces students to the science of learning using Shimamura’s MARGE framework, integrating theories of motivation, working memory, cognitive load, schema formation, and retrieval practice. Students apply evidence-based strategies to their own learning, and evaluate their effectiveness, fostering metacognitive awareness and ownership of learning. Evaluation demonstrates positive impact. Qualitative analysis of student reflections indicates increased confidence and transfer of learning strategies across subjects. Quantitative analysis shows statistically significant improvement in psychology attainment, with improvements or stability observed across other core subjects. Replication of the approach within a Year 10 biology class resulted in a statistically significant improvement in attainment. The findings indicate that explicitly teaching the science of learning can strengthen learner agency, support academic progress, and inform evidence-informed curriculum design and professional practice.

works.title: Launching with Intent: How Three Simple Classroom Modifications Raised Assessment Scores by 10%
works.venue: Teaching Social Studies in the Peach State
works.abstract: This action research study evaluated the impact of three targeted instructional modifications designed to address a 9% decline in proficient and distinguished student performance on the Georgia Milestones End-of-Course (EOC) Assessment in High School U.S. History. Building upon district leadership initiatives, an instructional team implemented a triad of evidence-based interventions across 15 units: (a) transitioning from digital assessment platforms to traditional paper-and-pencil testing to protect academic integrity, (b) implementing "Launching with Intent" vocabulary bell-ringers utilizing Frayer models and interactive word walls, and (c) embedding weekly 10-item formative unit quizzes to leverage retrieval practice and memory reconsolidation. Comparative data analysis demonstrated a 10 percentage point increase across internal summative assessments compared to the prior cohort, a trajectory subsequently substantiated by official statewide comparative performance metrics. These findings suggest that pairing paper-based summative testing with structured vocabulary scaffolds and frequent retrieval practice offers a sustainable, highly replicable framework for elevating secondary social studies achievement on high-stakes state assessments.

works.title: The disfluency effect revisited: processing demands moderate memory performance
works.abstract: "Desirable difficulties" describe encoding conditions that enhance memory. Recently, this principle has been extended to perceptual difficulties, such as hard-to-read fonts. Although several studies report a memory benefit of disfluency, other findings fail to replicate this effect or even show reversals, consistent with a resource-sharing account. The present study examined whether processing demands moderate the disfluency effect. We hypothesised that under low processing demands, disfluent fonts engage additional encoding processes, whereas under high demands, cognitive resources are consumed by processing disfluency itself. Across three experiments, participants performed word classification tasks with easy-to-read or hard-to-read fonts followed by a free recall test. In Experiment 1, using a task-switching procedure, hard-to-read font did not significantly affect recall performance, although it was descriptively higher for easy-to-read font. In Experiment 2, a low-demanding single-task procedure revealed no effect of font. In Experiment 3, hard-to-read font benefited recall in a low-demanding two-option, but not in a high-demanding four-option task, suggesting that processing demands moderated the disfluency effect. Together, the results imply that under sufficiently low processing demands, a disfluent font can benefit memory, in line with the desirable difficulties account. However, the findings suggest that this benefit may be difficult to reliably elicit.

works.title: ADHD symptoms and efficient learning strategies in college students: the parallel mediating roles of motivation and mind-wandering
works.abstract: A questionnaire survey was conducted among college students from a university in Sichuan Province to examine the relationship between ADHD symptoms and the use of efficient learning strategies, with a focus on the parallel mediating roles of learning motivation and mind-wandering. Of the 919 questionnaires distributed, 730 valid responses (N = 730) were retained for analysis. Structural equation modeling with bootstrap confidence intervals indicated that learning motivation and mind-wandering acted as parallel mediators in the relationship between ADHD symptoms and strategy use, with both learning motivation and mind-wandering showing negative indirect effects (learning motivation: β = -0.130, 95% CI [-0.196, -0.061]; mind-wandering: β = -0.107, 95% CI [-0.198, -0.027]). The direct effect of ADHD symptoms on strategy use was non-significant (β = -0.056, 95% CI [-0.160, 0.053]), whereas both indirect effects were statistically significant, albeit with small-to-moderate effect sizes. These findings contribute to understanding the associated mechanisms of academic difficulties in college students with elevated ADHD symptoms, particularly highlighting the dual pathways of motivation and mind-wandering. The study offers tentative theoretical implications and suggests directions for future intervention research (e.g., motivational reinforcement, attentional training); given the small-to-moderate absolute magnitudes of the indirect effects, these practical implications should be interpreted with caution pending replication.

works.title: Telling Students to Evaluate Does Not Make It Happen: Task Stage, Offloading Tendency, and Error Detection in AI-Assisted Student Writing
works.abstract: Instructors can prescribe which part of a writing task a student may delegate to generative AI, but not how the student works. This four-arm randomised experiment separated them. At Site A, 744 undergraduates were randomised to one of four divisions of labour across four rounds of report writing-AI drafts and the student evaluates and revises; the student drafts and AI evaluates; the student drafts, AI revises, and the student adjudicates each change; no AI-with all AI withdrawn at Week 6 post-test, immediately after the final round (639 completed). A reduced three-arm replication at Site B randomised 126 students (109 completed). Both arrangements in which the student judged AI-produced text outperformed the arrangement in which AI judged student-produced text and the no-AI control (d = 0.35 to 0.36), whereas having AI evaluate was equivalent to no AI. The benefit was unevenly distributed (arm × tendency F(3, 629) = 7.25, p < 0.001), and logs showed students high in dependent tendency re-outsourcing their assigned evaluation (b = 0.072, p < 0.001). Satisfaction carried no information about error detection (r = 0.015), while self-rated quality was weakly associated with writing performance. Prescribing a division of labour governs the assignment, not the cognition.

works.title: Why Wait? A Meta-Analysis of Task and Sample Moderators of Children’s Performance on the Marshmallow Test
works.abstract: The marshmallow test is the most well-known behavioral assessment of delay of gratification in children and performance on the test is associated with several later life outcomes. Yet studies vary considerably in their samples and implementation of the task. This meta-analysis examined whether task and sample characteristics moderate children’s waiting patterns. Multilevel meta-regressions synthesized 119 samples from 86 published and unpublished studies conducted across six continents (most from North America) with maximum waiting periods ranging from 7 to 25 minutes. Outcomes were mean wait time, proportion of children waiting the full delay period, and proportion excluded from analyses. Older children waited longer and were more likely to complete the full delay. Samples characterized as lower socioeconomic status had shorter mean wait times, although socioeconomic status was not associated with waiting the full delay period. Allowing children to choose the reward and providing an explanation for the experimenter’s delayed return were unrelated to waiting, and Bayesian model comparisons provided moderate evidence for the null with respect to these moderators. Most other coded procedural characteristics were also unrelated to waiting. Longer maximum task durations were associated with longer mean wait times but lower odds of completing the full delay and greater odds of exclusion. Publication year was positively associated with mean wait time, consistent with prior research, although this association varied by sample age and maximum task duration. Overall, children’s waiting was relatively consistent across many procedural variations, while age, socioeconomic context, and task duration emerged as important sources of variation.

works.title: Pavlovian Conditioning and Self-Control: From Laboratory to Classroom Application
works.abstract: Impulsive choice, the preference for a smaller-sooner reward (SSR) over a larger-later reward (LLR), is associated with various challenging behaviors (e.g., gambling and substance-used disorders). Many interventions can reduce impulsive choice but those that produce long-lasting effects typically require long training durations or are difficult to implement in applied settings. This dissertation evaluated a novel Pavlovian training approach designed to promote self-control. In Experiment 1, procedures from Mahmoudi and Madden (2024) were replicated in the laboratory with the addition of a truly random control group. The study also assessed whether presenting the conditioned stimulus (CS) before a choice would increase preference for the LLR compared to when the CS is presented both before choice and during the delay to the LLR. Experiment 2 adapted the Pavlovian training program in two kindergarten classrooms and later used the CS to assess if children would wait for a novel toy. Evidence for Pavlovian conditioned was limited in the first classroom but showed promising results in the second, following procedural modification. Although not consistent across all participants, presenting them during the delay reduced the frequency of challenging behavior.

works.title: Revisiting patience and achievement: evidence from matched parent–child preferences
works.abstract: This paper examines whether children’s time preferences independently predict academic achievement using matched incentivized measures for parents and children linked to standardized mathematics performance. Reduced-form regressions replicate prior findings that more patient children perform better academically. However, once parental time preferences are included, children’s patience no longer predicts achievement, while parental patience remains strongly significant across specifications. These results suggest that previously documented links between children’s time preferences and academic performance may reflect intergenerational behavioral transmission or household inputs rather than child-specific traits. The findings highlight the importance of jointly modeling parent and child characteristics when studying non-cognitive skill formation.

works.title: The Development of Social-Emotional Skills in Early Education : New Approaches to Old Questions
works.abstract: Social-emotional skills-encompassing the ways individuals manage relationships, regulate emotions, and direct their own behavior-predict outcomes across education, employment, mental health, and civic engagement, making their early development a matter of both individual and societal concern.Although theoretical frameworks including bioecological theory, attachment theory, and social learning theory suggest that ECEC is an important context for fostering these skills, empirical findings have been inconsistent.This may partly reflect limited attention to children's individual characteristics as moderators of ECEC effects, an over-reliance on questionnaire-based measures of behavioral tendencies rather than direct assessments of capacities, and a disproportionate focus on the United States.Three empirical studies conducted in Germany and German-speaking Switzerland addressed these gaps.Study 1 examined whether interaction quality in German ECEC predicted changes in children's learning and social behavior, and whether emotion regulation moderated this association.Using CLASS Toddler in a sample of 65 children from nine ECEC groups, higher engaged support for learning predicted improvements in positive learning behavior-particularly for children with lower emotion regulation, who showed greater sensitivity to both low-and high-quality settings.This pattern is consistent with the Differential Susceptibility Hypothesis, though the data do not rule out the simpler Dual-Risk Model, and replication in larger samples is needed to distinguish between them.Study 2 responded to calls for direct assessments of social-emotional skills by developing and validating the Behavioral Assessment of Social-Emotional Skills (BASES) in a sample of 141 four-to eight-year-olds in Switzerland.Rather than relying on questionnaires, BASES directly observes children's capacities across five domains: social engagement, collaboration, task performance, emotional regulation, and open-mindedness (creativity).Children solve standardized tasks in small peer groups, and trained raters evaluate their performance against detailed behavioral markers.BASES demonstrated good to excellent objectivity across most constructs, strong reliability, good factorial validity, and-crucially-stronger associations with children's age than a parallel teacher-reported questionnaire, suggesting greater sensitivity to developmental change.Study 3 applied BASES in a large representative sample of 1,246 Swiss kindergarten children to examine whether type, weekly hours, duration, and interaction quality in ECEC before kindergarten predicted later social-emotional skills.More weekly hours and longer duration in daycare centers were associated with better collaboration and social engagement, and children with the longest daycare durations also scored highest in emotional regulation and task performance.Playgroup attendance showed fewer associations, likely reflecting its more limited scope.Interaction quality, observed with CLASS Toddler in a subsample of 53 children, was not significantly associated with any outcome.Alongside ECEC effects, family background variables-household income, parental education, and family language-emerged as consistent predictors of children's social-emotional skills, highlighting the broader socioeconomic context in which ECEC operates.Taken together, the findings suggest that global measures of caregiver-child interaction quality may be insufficient to explain social-emotional development-which, like cognitive development, may require domain-specific teaching and support rather than a warm climate alone.Current tools further assess what caregivers typically do rather than what they are capable of, and more individualized, capacityoriented measures of both interaction quality and caregiver competence could help untangle contributions that group-level scores obscure.The positive associations between daycare center dosage and interpersonal skills additionally poi

works.title: Delayed gratification across 22 Countries: A cross-national analysis of demographic variation and childhood predictors
How Often Are Constraints on Generality (COGs) Discussed? A Look at Articles Published in Four Psychology Journals 2018-2022
works.abstract: Constraints on Generality statements (COGs, Simons, et al., 2017) address the boundary conditions of study findings, informing readers of the participant populations and methodological and social/cultural/historical contexts within which the reported phenomena are expected to occur. This in turn informs readers of the contexts in which additional studies are needed, facilitating cumulative science. Knowledge of boundary conditions is also crucial for conducting meaningful direct replications of findings (Simons, et al., 2018). In our review of 282 articles, we found that 6 included a separate COG subsection. The proportion of articles that contained any explicit COG statements anywhere in the discussion section ranged from 5% to 40% across the four journals we examined. This proportion was higher in journals whose editors publicly encouraged inclusion of COGs. We believe continued monitoring of the inclusion of COGs would be beneficial not only in psychology but also for other scientific disciplines.

works.title: The Marshmallow Test and Contemporary Issues in Psychology
works.abstract: Despite being one of the most well-known laboratory-based tasks in psychology, certain methodological and theoretical considerations surrounding the marshmallow test have gone largely unstudied until recently. These considerations reflect gaps in the delay of gratification literature and broader contemporary issues concerning the replicability of seminal findings and the lack of an agreed upon theoretical framework in the field. Accordingly, my dissertation uses the classic marshmallow test to explore the contemporary issues of replication and theory in psychology in a series of three studies. In Study 1, the marshmallow test is at the center of a case study unpacking the nuances of direct and conceptual replication; a tool designed to support ongoing replication efforts is proposed. Study 2 executes a full-scale replication of the paradigm from the case study, and introduces a methodological extension to improve the paradigm’s experimental rigour while making it amenable to an evolutionary–developmental framework. Finally, Study 3 applies an evolutionary–developmental framework to examine how this perspective might help account for individual differences in marshmallow test behavior. Through these three studies, my dissertation provides an example of how engaging in replication and applying an evolutionary–developmental framework to the marshmallow test literature to inform outstanding theoretical questions in psychology might be mutually beneficial endeavors.

works.title: Early childhood executive function predicts concurrent and later social and behavioral outcomes: A review and meta-analysis.
works.abstract: Executive function (EF), the set of mental processes and skills involved in goal-oriented planning, organizing, and controlling behavior, is believed to support child development across many domains of life. However, although ample evidence suggests a relation between childhood EF and academic skills, it is less clear what its role is in domains beyond academics. We report a meta-analysis of relations between early childhood EF (assessed at 36-60 months of age) and social, health, and behavioral outcomes assessed concurrently and longitudinally (1,459 effect sizes, 158 studies, n = 144,642). No significant relations were found between EF and health outcomes. EF was concurrently associated with emotion understanding and regulation, prosocial skills, peer acceptance, and skill at lying. Both concurrently and longitudinally, EF was positively associated with peer acceptance, adaptive classroom behavior, and social competence, and negatively associated with internalizing and externalizing problems, and inattention and hyperactivity. For adolescent outcomes, only the relation between EF and internalizing could be meta-analyzed, and no significant relation was found between these variables. The magnitude of effect sizes varied, with absolute values ranging from r = .02 to .30. Moderator analyses indicated the relation between EF and behavioral outcomes varied by outcome, but there was no such finding for EF and social or health outcomes. EF was more strongly associated with teacher- versus parent-reported behavioral problems. There was little evidence that quality indicators affected effect sizes. There was also little evidence of publication bias. Overall, our results are consistent with the possibility of broad relevance of EF for child development; yet, future research should provide stronger causal tests of hypothesized relations between EF and outcomes to better understand the nature of EF and whether fostering it can promote healthy development.
